newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks stagger at finish of last 1996 session.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks stagger at finish of last 1996 session.

text.p: The Dow industrials on Tuesday finished with their sharpest decline since July, pummeled by a weak bond market and a flurry of last-minute profit-taking and program trading.
The Dow industrials fell 101 points to close the last session of 1996 unofficially at 6448.
A large portion of the Dow's losses came in the last hour of trading, well after stocks had been dealt a body blow by a pair of economic indicators that roiled the bond market.

The Commerce Department reported a greater-than-expected 14.2 percent rise in sales of single-family homes in November, while the Conference Board's December consumer-confidence index jumped by more than four points to 113.8. Both reports suggested the U.S. economy was stronger than many had thought.
The news sent the price of the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond sliding 1-9/32, pushing the yield up to 6.64 percent in an abbreviated trading session.
"During the entire rally this year, stocks have moved up in tandem with bonds," said Larry Wachtel, a market analyst at Prudential Securities. "Today, the long bond got whacked."

Late in the session, a sell program touched off a second round of losses, prompting index-arbitrage trading curbs on the New York Stock Exchange and triggering a scramble of selling to protect profits.
"By late in the day, the primary people are already working on their egg nog," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
"The people that are left for the most part are only authorized to sell in order to take profits, not to commit new capital," Orlando said. "That creates a downward bias."

The selling was largely focused on the large-cap, blue chip stocks that have far outperformed the rest of the market in the last couple of months. The S&P 500 fell nearly two percent, while the Nasdaq Composite eked out a small gain.

The decline on Tuesday put a small dent in the Dow's 1996 rise. Even so, the average ended the year about 1331 points, or 26 percent, higher than it began. Coupled with its 1995 performance, the Dow has climbed more than 68 percent over the last two years.
Financial issues were broadly weaker, reflecting the decline in bond prices. Citicorp fell 3-3/4 to 103, NationsBank Corp dropped 3-1/4 to 97-3/4 and Wells Fargo and Co shed 6-3/4 to 269-3/4.

Among individual issues, Renaissance Hotel Group jumped 7-1/8 to 23-1/2 after agreeing to be acquired by hotel operator Doubletree Corp in a deal valued at $850 million. Shares in Doubletree fell 2-1/2 to 45.
Donnelly Corp rose 2-7/8 to 24-1/2 after Smith Barney started coverage of the company with a buy rating.
